quote: Anything a user can do in an app, an agent can also do. Then anything the app can do, the agent can do. Eventually, anything a developer can do—changing logic, fixing bugs, customizing behavior—will be something the agent handles on the user’s behalf.
author: Dan Shipper
context: Prediction 1 of 3, 'Agents become infrastructure'. A staged claim about how software gets built; the first stage (agents can do anything a user can in an app) is the checkable 2026 part, the 'eventually' stage has no date.

quote: 2026 is when agents go mainstream.
author: Kieran Klaassen
context: Prediction 1 of 3. Editor's one-line rendering of Klaassen's view ('Kieran puts it simply'), not a direct quote. 'Mainstream' is undefined; the bars will need an adoption measure.

quote: Natalia thinks the most advanced companies will have agentic workflows embedded in daily operations by year’s end
author: Natalia Quintero
context: Prediction 1 of 3. Editor's paraphrase of Quintero (Every's head of consulting). Leading companies run agentic workflows in day-to-day operations by end of 2026, with finance named as the example industry.

quote: AI will allow tech-forward firms to synthesize an even broader amount of information. This will change the industry, similar to the way quantitative finance changed the industry.
author: Natalia Quintero
context: Prediction 1 of 3, direct quote about finance. A structural-change claim with no date; the 2026 reading is that AI-driven synthesis becomes a recognised competitive factor in finance during the year.

quote: Dan predicts a third kind of engineer: agentic engineers who fully delegate implementation to AI and move up a level to managing and orchestrating agents.
author: Dan Shipper
context: Prediction 2 of 3, 'New roles are emerging'. Editor's paraphrase. A recognised job category of engineers who direct agents rather than write code emerges in 2026.

quote: Kate expects most companies to have at least one dedicated role focused on building and maintaining internal AI systems by 2026—“someone whose job is to continuously optimize how the organization uses AI.”
author: Kate Lee
context: Prediction 2 of 3. Editor's paraphrase plus a direct quote. 'Most companies' is the checkable element; the bars will need a survey or job-posting measure.

quote: There’s a whole class of highly creative, highly visual people who have been held back from making full experiences because they can’t code. Now they’re going to be able to code.
author: Dan Shipper
context: Prediction 3 of 3, 'Designers become superheroes'. Designers and other non-coders ship working software with AI tools in 2026.

quote: A mass-market robotic pet succeeds by the end of 2026.
author: Willie Williams
context: The wildcard prediction, stated as the editor's rendering of Williams's view. He names Moflin as the one to watch. 'Succeeds' is undefined.

quote: I think AI progress is still really fast and it's kind of mind-blowing where where we are now versus where we were a year ago. And I think that will be the case in at the end of 2026. I think we'll be sitting here being like, "Wow, it's like actually a lot better."
author: Dan Shipper
context: At the end of 2026 AI capability will be noticeably better than at the end of 2025; no metric is named, so 'a lot better' is a judgement call.

quote: AGI, however you define that, is a lot more complicated and hard than we thought. And we will not have AGI in 2027.
author: Dan Shipper
context: No AGI by 2027; the horizon is a year past the target year and AGI is explicitly left undefined, so a 2026 check can only falsify it if AGI is widely agreed to have arrived.

quote: if you are an engineer who wants to incorporate AI into your process but doesn't want to reinvent the skill of software engineering there's going to be a home and a job for you for a very long time.
author: Dan Shipper
context: Traditional engineers who use AI as an accelerant will keep having jobs; 'a very long time' has no end date, so a 2026 check is only whether that job category visibly persisted.

quote: What we're doing next year is um we're going to build this like unified memory and context layer where we have um we have a bunch of uh basically we can collect everything everything that you care about and who you are into one place and all of the apps and all the content can take that into account as they work with you.
author: Dan Shipper
context: Every will ship a unified memory and context layer across its apps in 2026; this is a company plan rather than an industry forecast.

quote: I think we'll hire next year, but I don't think we're going to hire a ton. Like the whole thing is like keep it small.
author: Dan Shipper
context: Every will add staff in 2026 but not many, staying a small company; 'a ton' is undefined (they were at about 20 people).

quote: agentic development will be maybe by the end of the year inside of the app that you're actually using.
author: Brandon Gell
context: By the end of 2026 users will be able to request features or bug fixes from inside an app and have an agent write and ship the code; unclear whether this means any shipping product or broad availability.

quote: I think that that's going to be broadly distributed like especially that first level is going to be a broadly distributed paradigm in a year that no one's really talking about right now except for except for anthropic I think anthropic has nailed this but everyone else is going to be doing it
author: Dan Shipper
context: Within a year agent-native level 1 (anything a user can do in an app the agent can do) becomes a widely adopted paradigm beyond Anthropic; 'anthropic' is lowercase in the captions. Spoken form of c1; not graded separately to avoid double counting.

quote: I think all these designers are just going to like start going crazy and it's going to become this new archetype of like really interesting builder.
author: Dan Shipper
context: Designers and visual creatives will start vibe coding their own tools and apps at scale, forming a recognised new builder archetype (companion page heading: designers will start building their own tools). Spoken form of c7; not graded separately to avoid double counting.

quote: they might need to abstract it away from the code so that like the average person doesn't get scared like going near code.
author: Brandon Gell
context: AI coding tools like Cursor will need to hide the code to reach designers at scale; phrased as a 'might need to', so it is a soft prediction about product direction.

quote: I think midterms are going to be like kind of scary. Um because I think there's going to be deep fakes, which used to be a really scary word and now nobody talks about nobody says deep fake anymore.
author: Brandon Gell
context: AI deepfakes will be a significant, alarming feature of the 2026 US midterm elections.

quote: So, I think like that's my doom or take is something's going to happen with elections that like that's that's that's what will trigger um you know some sort of label that's like made with AI.
author: Brandon Gell
context: An election-related AI incident will force social media platforms to adopt 'made with AI' labelling; he says if not by the midterms then by the next presidential election, so the horizon is 2028 at the latest. 'doom or take' is the captions' mishearing of 'doomer take'.

quote: I think that I think that scary stuff is going to happen where fake videos are made like deep, you know, the nature of the word deep fake came from like people doing like really grotesque things that like they didn't actually do, but AI made it look like they they did that.
author: Brandon Gell
context: Fabricated AI videos showing politicians doing things they did not do will appear during the 2026 election cycle; he later says this 'is going to happen 100%'.

quote: It's like a it's a third thing and I think that's going to be a big deal in in in 2026.
author: Dan Shipper
context: A third category of software builder, 'agentic engineers' or 'compound engineers' who delegate all coding to agents and never read code, becomes a big deal in 2026; 'big deal' is undefined. Spoken form of c5; not graded separately to avoid double counting.

quote: if you then zoom out though that kind that style of engineering is going to be on a pretty slow and steady decline.
author: Dan Shipper
context: Traditional software engineering with AI as an accelerant begins a slow, steady decline (newspaper-industry analogy); a slow decline is hard to confirm or deny within one year.

quote: Um, and if you look at the growth, the growth will be in this new kind of engineering in this new kind of engineering work.
author: Dan Shipper
context: Growth in software engineering employment or activity will come from agent-directing engineering rather than traditional coding.

quote: if you're, for example, a new grad and you're choosing between what what kind of stuff you're going to do, I think you're probably going to be more likely to to choose this third path.
author: Dan Shipper
context: New graduates will be more likely to choose the agentic-engineering path than traditional coding.

quote: um I I think there are a lot of people will pop up to like serve that need for kids that are not being served by universities.
author: Brandon Gell
context: Many new education providers will appear to teach AI-era software skills that universities are not teaching.

quote: I think we will definitely see um layoffs that companies blame on AI um in 2026
author: Dan Shipper
context: In 2026 companies will announce layoffs and publicly attribute them to AI.

quote: and I think mostly they will not be actually AI related they will be about the underlying business but they'll use AI as a good excuse.
author: Dan Shipper
context: Most 2026 layoffs blamed on AI will really be driven by underlying business problems, with AI used as cover; judging the true cause is inherently contestable.

quote: I would guess that they will find it valuable this year. Um specifically because coding agents are good enough that once they make their way into Excel in a widely distributed way
author: Dan Shipper
context: Non-technical knowledge workers (the example is a deal-desk analyst living in Excel) will find AI genuinely valuable at work in 2026 once coding-agent capability is widely distributed inside Excel.

quote: So I think that's going to actually happen a lot more in in 2026 is is we're going to um use training approaches and architectures that allow them to like go off and do stuff.
author: Dan Shipper
context: In 2026 labs will adopt training approaches and architectures that give agents more independence (loosening obedience-style alignment); the speaker calls it 'a very vague prediction'.

quote: And I think, shockingly, the most addictive technology of 2026—the narrative we might be talking about at the end of the year—is how addictive it is to just make things.
author: Dan Shipper
context: By end of 2026 the dominant tech-addiction narrative will be about compulsive making with AI coding tools (he adds that everyone will be prompting Claude Code), not social media.

quote: And I think that’s going to hamper their product direction and velocity in a way that—if we look back in a couple years—we might say: that was an interesting era. It’s still a widely distributed piece of software, but it’s not the next-generation thing that we thought it was.
author: Dan Shipper
context: Cursor is the coding-agent leader most likely to stumble, caught between the IDE-plus-AI paradigm and the Claude Code paradigm; the stated horizon is 'a couple years', so an end-2026 check is partial.

quote: But I think next year is going to be much more negative on AI than this year, in general popular discourse.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: Popular discourse about AI in 2026 will be much more negative than in 2025. Hoffman: 2026 discourse much more negative on AI. Pinned as a guest claim for contrast with the hosts' optimism.

quote: And so the meme is going to be: Oh, college students aren’t going to get hired because of AI. The meme is going to be: Electricity prices are going up because of AI. The meme is going to be: The price of eggs is going up because of AI.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: AI becomes the catch-all scapegoat in 2026 public discourse, blamed for graduate unemployment, electricity prices and inflation regardless of actual cause.

quote: But AI is going to start impacting things. So it moves from, call it, 98–99 percent fictional to 90 percent fictional.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: AI's real share of the employment and economic effects attributed to it rises in 2026 from roughly 1-2 percent to roughly 10 percent; the numbers are rhetorical, not measured.

quote: I think that will happen. I’m going to create some more records, and I think that will be the case.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: Hoffman expects to receive public backlash from artists and creatives for making more AI-generated music records in 2026, having gotten none for his AI Christmas record.

quote: But what I think 2026 will be is how we move from this basis of agentic coding agents to agents in everything else. I think there’s going to be a whole bunch of that.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: In 2026 agents break out of coding into other domains of knowledge work.

quote: For example: call it 10x to 100x more people will experience what it is to have their computer running separately from them—doing something productive for them—as they walk away to go get coffee, and then come back.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: The number of people who have experienced an agent working autonomously on their computer grows 10x to 100x in 2026; the baseline is unstated.

quote: I think orchestration is the thing. I don’t think it’ll be March 2026. I think it’ll be more like Q4 2026—or growing into that—and then maybe even more intensively in 2027.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: Orchestration of multiple agents by a human becomes the defining pattern of knowledge work, arriving around Q4 2026 rather than early in the year, and more intensively in 2027.

quote: Well, I think it’s one of the skills OpenAI is going to pick up.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: OpenAI will respond to Anthropic's lead and build coding tools aimed at AI-native engineers who orchestrate agents without reading code.

quote: But what I would predict strongly is that the horses that are leading now will still be neck and neck.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: At the end of 2026 the current coding-agent leaders (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Cursor and peers) will still be close competitors with no clear runaway winner.

quote: I don’t think any of the horses that are in the race will particularly stumble. I don’t think you’ll look up and go, Wow, I thought Cursor was fantastic—and it’s just gone.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: None of the current coding-agent leaders will collapse or exit the market during 2026. Hoffman: none of the coding-agent leaders will stumble. Pinned because it directly contradicts Shipper's own Cursor call (c31).

quote: I think the gap will be even more stunning—the fact that you haven’t really internalized what this coding amplification—and everything it implies—means. And I think that will play out more.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: Apple's gap versus AI leaders will widen further in 2026 because it has not internalised coding amplification.

quote: I’m more curious about what one or two superstars will get into the mix more. Will Replit become more general? Will Lovable become more general? Will it be those—or will it be something else? And with pretty high probability, something will surprise us here.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: With high probability a surprise entrant or a company like Replit or Lovable becomes a general coding-agent contender in 2026; 'surprise' is loosely defined.

quote: So yes: I think it’ll be much more intensely positive. And it’ll be positive because we’ll have two groups of things in real deployment.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: By the end of 2026 the narrative on enterprise AI deployments flips from disappointing to much more positive, driven by real deployments.

quote: if you’re a company that wants to be a thriving, growing concern, evolving with the times, you will need to be recording every single meeting and using agents on it to amplify your work process. And by the end of 2026, if you’re not doing it, that’s because you’re making excuses.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: By end of 2026 recording every meeting and running agents on it is standard practice at thriving companies; partly normative, so the checkable part is whether the practice became widespread.

quote: And two: you will start systematically deploying groups of agents to solve various problems.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: Enterprises begin systematically deploying groups of agents to solve problems during 2026 (he says it will not kick off in Q1 but grow through the year).

quote: I think what we’ll see more of in 2026 is a combination of parallelization, longer workflows, and orchestration—which is part of the reason I like getting to a clearer realization of what agents are.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: The 2026 version of AGI is parallelised agents, longer workflows and human orchestration (one person with a team of agents) applied beyond coding, rather than a new kind of model.

quote: I don’t think we’ll have the press-a-button, fully human-capable software engineer—I’m ready to do the thing you asked me to do—which is the sci-fi version people are looking for.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: No fully autonomous human-equivalent software engineer agent arrives in 2026; instead human engineers run teams of agents that cross-check each other.

quote: I think we’ll be doing a lot more in-depth modeling of things that are not close to human language. For example: biology.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: Generative AI model-building increasingly targets non-language domains in 2026, with biology (treated as a language) the most natural place it shows up; Hoffman notes his stake via Manas AI, which the transcript spells 'Manus'.

quote: I don’t know if 2026 will be the full hit there. There’s a probabilistic curve. But it wouldn’t surprise me if you get the equivalent of a move 37—something around biology.
author: Reid Hoffman
context: A 'move 37' breakthrough in AI-driven biology (a surprising molecule or research direction) may arrive in 2026; he later puts it as a research possibility with a 27 percent probability, so it is explicitly hedged.

quote: Hoffman’s bets: Agents will break out of coding into everything else.
author: Reid Hoffman (restated by Every Staff)
context: Every's restatement of Hoffman's first bet: agents move beyond coding into other domains in 2026.

quote: One person directing agents will have the capacity of an entire team—his working definition of AGI for 2026.
author: Reid Hoffman (restated by Every Staff)
context: Every's restatement: in 2026 a single person orchestrating agents has the output capacity of a whole team.

quote: Enterprises that don’t deploy agents at every meeting will fall behind.
author: Reid Hoffman (restated by Every Staff)
context: Every's restatement: companies not running agents on every meeting will fall behind in 2026; a stronger wording than Hoffman's own 'making excuses' line.

quote: Discourse will get uglier even as the tools improve.
author: Reid Hoffman (restated by Every Staff)
context: Every's restatement: public discourse on AI gets more negative in 2026 while the tools keep getting better.

quote: And biology—treated as a language to model molecules—will be the next frontier.
author: Reid Hoffman (restated by Every Staff)
context: Every's restatement: biology modelled as a language becomes AI's next frontier; 'next frontier' has no fixed date.

quote: Read this for the architecture that’s replacing traditional software development.
author: Every Staff
context: Every's own claim, embedded in a reading blurb, that agent-native architecture is replacing traditional software development; a trend assertion rather than a dated forecast.

quote: This opens up a new field: software that works the way Claude Code works, applied to categories far beyond coding.
author: Dan Shipper
context: Agent-native software (an agent with tools in a loop) spreads to categories far beyond coding; the essay is a design document and this is its only forward-looking claim, undated and coauthored with Claude.

quote: Autonomous loops that ship improvements while you sleep
author: Vibe Code Camp participants (reported by Katie Parrott)
context: Listed under 'What's next' from 16 Vibe Code Camp speakers: autonomous agent loops that analyse metrics and ship improvements overnight become common; Every staff summarised the campers' views, so attribution is to the campers.

quote: Vibe coded software running in production at scale
author: Vibe Code Camp participants (reported by Katie Parrott)
context: Listed under 'What's next': vibe-coded software runs in production at scale; 'at scale' is undefined.

quote: I suggested to a group of fellow seekers that we’ll likely create consciousness in machines—and soon.
author: Ashwin Sharma
context: Machine consciousness is likely to be created soon; 'soon' has no date and consciousness has no agreed test, so this is close to uncheckable.
